subject: english-language
title: The Classroom IRF
welcome_lead: Every classroom dialogue follows a hidden script. Sinclair and Coulthard cracked it open: Initiation, Response, Feedback.
meta_desc: Sinclair & Coulthard's IRF, turn-taking and adjacency pairs at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have unmasked the IRF — the invisible chassis of classroom talk.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Recording Birmingham classrooms, Sinclair and Coulthard found a tight pattern: teacher asks a known-answer question, a pupil responds, and the teacher evaluates.

This IRF structure is the basic unit of pedagogic discourse, distinguishing classrooms from ordinary conversation.

Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson's 1974 paper modelled turn allocation. At a TRP the current speaker may select the next, or any other participant may self-select.

The system minimises gap and overlap while still permitting flexibility — a feat of micro-coordination.

If A invites B, B's preferred response is acceptance — immediate, brief, unmarked. A refusal is dispreferred: delayed, prefaced with well, hedged with accounts.

This asymmetry shows social structure embedded in conversational sequence.

options: Adjacency pairs are pairs of synonyms in vocabulary lists.
Adjacency pairs are two people who sit next to each other while talking.
